title: Velocity–Time and Distance–Time Graphs
standard_text: Interpret the gradient at a point on a curve as the instantaneous rate of change; calculate or estimate gradients of graphs and areas under graphs (including velocity–time and distance–time graphs) and interpret results in context.
meta_desc: Free Year 11 GCSE maths worksheets on velocity–time graphs: acceleration from the gradient, distance from the area, distance–time graphs and estimating areas with trapezia. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: On a distance–time graph, the gradient is the speed.
body_html:
How it works

On a velocity–time graph, the gradient is the acceleration (a downward slope is a deceleration) and the area under the graph is the distance travelled. Split the area into triangles, rectangles and trapezia.

On a distance–time graph, the gradient is the speed and a horizontal line means the object is not moving. For a curve, estimate the area with trapezia.

Example

A car speeds up from 4 m/s to 16 m/s in 6 s. Find the acceleration.

(16 − 4) ÷ 6

Answer: 2 m/s²

Example

It does this at a steady rate. Find the distance travelled.

½ × (4 + 16) × 6

Answer: 60 m

Common mistakes

  • Reading the velocity as the distance.
  • Working out time ÷ velocity for the gradient.
  • Leaving out the time spent stopped in an average speed.

faq.q: What does the area under a velocity–time graph show?
faq.a: The distance travelled. Split it into triangles, rectangles and trapezia and add the areas.

faq.q: What does the gradient of a velocity–time graph show?
faq.a: The acceleration. A negative gradient is a deceleration and a horizontal line means constant velocity.

items.q: A motorbike's velocity changes uniformly from 16 m/s to 6 m/s in 10 seconds. Work out the deceleration.
items.e: Acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time = (6 − 16) ÷ 10 = −1 m/s².
